topics.title: Know number names and the count sequence forward

subtopics.title: Know number names and the count sequence forward

outcomes.text: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
Count forward beginning from any given number within the range of 0–100.
Write numbers from 0 to 20. Given a set of 0–20 objects, write a numeral to represent the quantity.

topics.title: Know number names and the count sequence backward

subtopics.title: Know number names and the count sequence backward

outcomes.text: Count backwards by ones from 20 to 0.
Count backwards beginning from any given number within the range of 0–20.

topics.title: Count to tell the number of objects

subtopics.title: Demonstrate awareness of the principles of counting

outcomes.text: Number names must be said in the standard order (sequencing).
Each object must be paired with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object (one-to-one correspondence).
The last number name said tells the number of objects counted, objects may be counted in any order (cardinality).
The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted (conservation of number).
Each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.

subtopics.title: Count to tell the number of objects

outcomes.text: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration. Given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.
Quickly recognize and name the quantity of up to 5 objects briefly shown in structured or unstructured arrangements without counting (perceptual subitizing).

topics.title: Compare numbers

subtopics.title: Compare numbers

outcomes.text: Determine whether the number of objects in one group of 1– 10 objects is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group of 1–10 objects. For example, using matching and counting strategies.
Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.

topics.title: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from

subtopics.title: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from

outcomes.text: Represent addition and subtraction situations in a variety of ways. For example, with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.

Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 in more than one way. For example, by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation, as in 5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1, and 5 = 2 + 2 + 1.
For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given numbers by using objects or drawings and record the answer with a drawing or equation.
By the end of kindergarten, flexibly, efficiently and accurately find all sums within 5. Note: Fluency of this standard is critical by the end of grade level.

outcomes.text: Add-to with result unknown.
Take-from with result unknown.
Put-together/take-apart with total unknown.
Put-together with both addends unknown.

subtopics.title: Fluently add and subtract within 5 using efficient mental strategies

outcomes.text: Counting on.

units.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

topics.title: Work with numbers 11–19 to gain foundations for place value

subtopics.title: Work with numbers 11–19 to gain foundations for place value

outcomes.text: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation. For example, 18 = 10 + 8; understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

topics.title: Describe and compare measurable attributes

subtopics.title: Describe and compare measurable attributes

outcomes.text: Describe several measurable attributes (for example, length, width, weight) of objects by using words such as short, long, small, big, heavy, light.

Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of"/"less of" the attribute and describe the difference. For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.

topics.title: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category

subtopics.title: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category

outcomes.text: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count. Limit category counts to be less than or equal to 10.

topics.title: Identify attributes and values of money

subtopics.title: Identify attributes and values of money

outcomes.text: Identify the penny and know the value is one cent. Count pennies up to 20.

topics.title: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres)

subtopics.title: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres)

outcomes.text: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, besides, in front of, behind, and next to.
Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.
Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, "flat") or three-dimensional ("solid").

topics.title: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes

subtopics.title: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes

outcomes.text: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in varied sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts and other attributes. For example, number of sides and vertices/corners and having sides of equal length.
Model shapes in the world by building shapes from components and drawing shapes. For example, sticks and clay balls.
Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes. For example, "Can you join these two triangles with full sides touching to make a rectangle?"

subtopics.title: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction. Standard Rigor S

outcomes.text: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20. For example, by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

topics.title: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction

subtopics.title: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction

outcomes.text: Apply properties of operations, (commutative and associative), as strategies to add and subtract. For example, Commutative property of addition, if 8 + 3 = 11 is known then, 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. Associative property of addition, to add, 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12.
Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem. For example, subtract 10 − 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

topics.title: Add and subtract within 20

subtopics.title: Use counting and subitizing strategies to explain addition and subtraction

outcomes.text: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (for example, by counting on 2 to add 2).

Use conceptual subitizing in unstructured arrangements with totals up to 10 and structured arrangements anchored to 5 or 10 (for example, 10 frames, double ten frames, math rack) with totals up to 20 to relate the compositions and decompositions to addition and subtraction.

subtopics.title: Add and subtract within 20

outcomes.text: Relate counting forward and backward to addition and subtraction, add or subtract 1 or 2.
By the end of Grade 1, flexibly, efficiently, and accurately find all sums within 10. Note: Fluency of this standard is critical by the end of grade level.

subtopics.title: Add and subtract within 20, using strategies such as:

outcomes.text: Counting on.
Making ten (for example, 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14).
Decomposing a number leading to a ten (for example, 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − 1 = 10 − 1 = 9).
Using the relationship between addition and subtraction (for example, knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 − 8 = 4).
Creating equivalent but easier or known sums (for example, adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
Counting up to subtract.

topics.title: Work with addition and subtraction equations

subtopics.title: Work with addition and subtraction equations

outcomes.text: Understand the meaning of the equal sign and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false. For example, which of the following equations is true and which is false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 − 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 3 = 5 + 2.

Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating to three whole numbers. For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ⎕ = 11, 5 = ⎕ − 3, 6 + 6 = ⎕.

topics.title: Extend the counting sequence

subtopics.title: Extend the counting sequence

outcomes.text: Count forward and backward starting with any given number within the range of 0–120, In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

topics.title: Understand place value

subtopics.title: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases

outcomes.text: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."
The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

subtopics.title: Understand place value

outcomes.text: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, using phrases as greater than, less than or equal to, connecting to the use of >, =, and < symbols.

topics.title: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract

subtopics.title: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract

outcomes.text: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.
Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10 to 90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10 to 90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; explain the reasoning used.

topics.title: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units

subtopics.title: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units

outcomes.text: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps. Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

topics.title: Work with time and money

subtopics.title: Work with time and money

outcomes.text: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.
Identify pennies and dimes and their values. Count a mixed collection of dimes and pennies to determine the cent value (total not to exceed 100 cents).

topics.title: Represent and interpret data

subtopics.title: Represent and interpret data

outcomes.text: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

topics.title: Reason with shapes and their attributes

subtopics.title: Reason with shapes and their attributes

outcomes.text: Distinguish between defining attributes (for example, triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (for example, color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or threedimensional shapes (cubes, rectangular prisms, cones and cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape. Students do not need to learn formal names for these shapes.

Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.
